html:
The Reconquista, "reconquest", is the name for the long series of wars in which the Christian kingdoms of northern Spain and Portugal took the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim al-Andalus, from the 700s to 1492.

After the Umayyad conquest of 711, only the mountains of the north stayed in Christian hands. There the small kingdom of Asturias grew into León, and new states formed: Navarre, Aragon, Castile and, in the 1100s, Portugal. They fought al-Andalus, but also each other, and often allied with Muslim rulers.

The main steps:

  • 1085: Alfonso VI of León and Castile took Toledo, the old Visigothic capital.
  • 1086 to 1200s: the Almoravids and then the Almohads came over from Morocco and held the line for a time.
  • 1212: a joint Christian army broke the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa.
  • 1236 to 1249: Castile took Córdoba and Seville, and Portugal took the Algarve.
  • 1492: Isabella and Ferdinand took the emirate of Granada, the last Muslim state.

The wars made Castile a society of frontier warriors and military orders, and shaped Spanish and Portuguese ideas of crusade. The year Granada fell, Spain expelled its Jews and Columbus sailed west. The word "Reconquista" itself became popular only in the 19th century.
sum: The Reconquista, "reconquest", is the name for the long series of wars in which the Christian kingdoms of northern Spain and Portugal took the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim al-Andalus, from the 700s to 1492.
